title: System Design Primers
subtitle: ByteByteGo System Design 101 · The System Design Primer
lego: The official instruction booklets. Flip through every page once before you try your own model.
summary: Two free, visual, community-maintained overviews of every standard brick and pattern. ByteByteGo's System Design 101 is a collection of one-page diagrams (how HTTPS works, CDN, caching and database choices). Donne Martin's System Design Primer is a structured syllabus with worked solutions and Anki decks.

sections.title: How to study them
items: Read one topic, close the tab, and redraw the diagram from memory in Excalidraw. Compare, then fix the gaps.
Map each topic to a card in this app, and put anything new in the card's Notes (N).

title: System Design Interview, Volumes 1 & 2
subtitle: Alex Xu (and Sahn Lam for Volume 2)
lego: The master-builder sets: complete models with step-by-step instructions and the reasoning behind each choice.
summary: Chapter-length walkthroughs of the classic builds, including the rate limiter, consistent hashing, key-value store, unique ID generator, URL shortener, web crawler, notification system, news feed, chat, search autocomplete, YouTube and Google Drive. Volume 2 adds proximity search, maps, payments, a stock exchange and more. Each follows a four-step framework: scope the problem, propose a high-level design, deep dive, wrap up.

sections.title: How to study it
items: Before each chapter, give yourself 45 minutes to design it cold. Then read it and list what you missed.
Rebuild the chapter's design as a Build card in your notes, with its steps and the bricks used.

title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
subtitle: Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly)
lego: The materials-science textbook: why each kind of plastic bends, snaps or holds under load.
summary: The deepest single book on the principles under the bricks: storage engines (LSM trees vs B-trees), encoding, replication, partitioning, transactions and isolation levels, the trouble with distributed systems, consistency and consensus, and batch and stream processing. It is where interview answers turn into real understanding.

sections.title: How to study it
items: One chapter a week. After each, write a one-paragraph explanation in Notes as if teaching a junior engineer.
Follow the chapter references into the papers listed under Foundational Papers.

title: Netflix: Datacenter Monolith → Cloud Microservices
subtitle: Netflix Tech Blog
lego: Watching a master builder take apart one giant brittle model and rebuild it as hundreds of small, replaceable sub-assemblies, while it stays on display the whole time.
summary: In 2008 a major database corruption stopped DVD shipments for three days. Netflix then spent about seven years moving from a monolith in its own datacenters to hundreds of microservices on AWS, finishing in 2016. Along the way it invented or popularized chaos engineering (Chaos Monkey), client-side load balancing, circuit breakers (Hystrix) and its own CDN (Open Connect).

sections.title: What to take away
items: Migrate incrementally: move one service or dataset at a time, with dual running and rollbacks.
Design for failure as the normal state, then prove it continuously in production.

title: Uber: Monolith → Microservices → Domains
subtitle: Uber Engineering blog
lego: Too many tiny sub-assemblies became impossible to navigate, so they were regrouped into labelled domains with a single door each.
summary: Uber split its early Python monolith into thousands of microservices to scale teams and cities. The complexity that followed led to Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture (DOMA): services grouped into domains and layers, each behind a gateway. Uber also moved from Postgres to MySQL for replication at scale, built the Schemaless datastore, and created H3 for geospatial indexing.

sections.title: What to take away
items: Microservices solve organizational scaling but create operational complexity, so group them deliberately.
Choose databases for their operational behaviour at scale (replication, upgrades), not just their features.

links.title: Why Uber Engineering switched from Postgres to MySQL
H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

title: Airbnb: Monorail → Service-Oriented Architecture
subtitle: The Airbnb Tech Blog
lego: One huge model everyone was editing at once got divided into owned sections with clear connection points.
summary: Airbnb's Ruby on Rails monolith ('Monorail') slowed hundreds of engineers who were deploying the same codebase. Over several years Airbnb migrated to a service-oriented architecture, with presentation, mid-tier and data services, an IDL-based service framework, and strict ownership. It also wrote widely read posts on payments idempotency and data infrastructure.

sections.title: What to take away
items: Carve out services along data ownership. A service should own its tables.
Invest in the platform (service framework, schemas, observability) before the migration, not after.

links.title: The Airbnb Tech Blog
links.note: Search for 'Building Services at Airbnb' and 'Avoiding Double Payments'

title: The Counterpoint: When Not to Split
subtitle: Segment's 'Goodbye Microservices'
lego: Sometimes the best build is fewer, larger bricks.
summary: Segment split its event-delivery pipeline into more than 140 per-destination microservices and queues. Operational load, library drift and on-call pain grew until it merged them back into one service with better testing. The lesson: architecture follows constraints (team size, traffic, change rate). A well-structured modular monolith is a legitimate end state.

sections.title: Ask before splitting
items: Do the parts need to scale, deploy or fail independently? Are different teams blocked on each other?
Can a module boundary inside one deployable give 80% of the benefit?

links.title: Goodbye Microservices: From 100s of problem children to 1 superstar

title: Google SRE Book & Amazon Builders' Library
subtitle: Free, production-hardened operating manuals
lego: The notes from people who keep the world's largest models standing day after day.
summary: Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (free online) covers SLOs, overload handling, cascading failures, load balancing and incident response. The Amazon Builders' Library is a set of essays by Amazon principal engineers on timeouts and retries, load shedding, caching, health checks, static stability and shuffle-sharding. Together they are the best free source on how systems behave under failure.

sections.title: Start with
items: SRE book: Service Level Objectives, Handling Overload, Addressing Cascading Failures.
Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter; Using load shedding; Caching challenges and strategies.

title: The Google File System (2003)
subtitle: Ghemawat, Gobioff, Leung · SOSP 2003
lego: The first mega storage bin built from thousands of cheap, breakable boxes.
summary: A single master holds metadata; chunkservers store 64 MB chunks, each replicated three times. The design assumes component failure is normal, optimizes for large sequential reads and record appends, and relaxes consistency. It is the ancestor of HDFS and of modern object and blob storage.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Separate the metadata path (the master) from the data path (clients talk directly to chunkservers).
Leases give one replica authority to order mutations.

title: MapReduce (2004)
subtitle: Dean & Ghemawat · OSDI 2004
lego: Give a thousand builders one simple instruction each, then gather their results in a sorted pile.
summary: A programming model in which users write map (emit key-value pairs) and reduce (combine the values for each key), and the framework handles partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance (re-running failed tasks) and stragglers (backup tasks). It launched Hadoop and the era of batch data processing.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Move computation to the data. Deterministic tasks can simply be re-executed on failure.

links.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (PDF)

title: Bigtable (2006)
subtitle: Chang et al. · OSDI 2006
lego: The first giant Bionicle: a sparse, sorted, ever-growing map split into tablets.
summary: A sparse, distributed, persistent, sorted map indexed by (row, column, timestamp). Tables split into tablets served by tablet servers; data is stored as SSTables on GFS, with Chubby for coordination. It inspired HBase and Cassandra's data model, and LSM-tree storage is now everywhere.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Write to a memtable and commit log, flush to immutable SSTables, and compact in the background. That is the LSM tree.
Row keys sorted lexicographically make row-key design the performance lever.

links.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (PDF)

title: Dynamo (2007)
subtitle: DeCandia et al. (Amazon) · SOSP 2007
lego: A shopping-cart store that would rather show a slightly old cart than no cart at all.
summary: An always-writable, highly available key-value store for Amazon's shopping cart. It combines consistent hashing with virtual nodes, replication to N nodes with tunable R and W quorums, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, vector clocks for conflict detection, Merkle trees for anti-entropy, and gossip for membership. It shaped Cassandra, Riak and the NoSQL movement.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Availability over consistency for business reasons: an 'add to cart' must never fail.
Push conflict resolution to reads, and to the application.

links.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (PDF)
Amazon DynamoDB (USENIX ATC 2022)
links.note: How the managed service differs from the 2007 design

title: The Log & Kafka (2011–2013)
subtitle: Jay Kreps (LinkedIn)
lego: The realization that the conveyor belt itself is the most important piece in the factory.
summary: An essay arguing that an append-only, totally ordered log is the unifying abstraction behind databases (write-ahead logs), replication, data integration and stream processing. Built at LinkedIn as Kafka, it became the backbone of event-driven architectures and change data capture.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Put every change on a log, and every other system becomes a materialized view of it.
Each consumer tracks its own offset, which is why a stream can replay and a queue can't.

links.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction

title: Spanner (2012)
subtitle: Corbett et al. (Google) · OSDI 2012
lego: A rigid LEGO grid stretched across the whole planet, kept in sync by atomic clocks.
summary: A globally distributed database with externally consistent (linearizable) transactions. TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty from GPS and atomic clocks, and commits wait out that uncertainty. Data is split into Paxos-replicated groups, and two-phase commit runs across groups. It showed that SQL, strong consistency and global scale can coexist, which inspired CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Bounded clock uncertainty plus commit-wait gives global ordering without a single leader.

title: Raft & Paxos: Consensus
subtitle: Ongaro & Ousterhout 2014 · Lamport 2001
lego: The rule five builders use to agree on the next brick even when some of them fall asleep.
summary: Consensus lets a cluster agree on an ordered log despite crashes, as long as a majority is up. Raft splits the problem into leader election, log replication and safety, and was designed to be understandable. It powers etcd (Kubernetes), Consul and CockroachDB. Paxos is the original, and 'Paxos Made Simple' is its short explanation.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Majority quorums: 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures. Terms (epochs) fence off stale leaders.

links.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)

title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook (2013)
subtitle: Nishtala et al. · NSDI 2013
lego: How to run the world's biggest arm's-reach shelf without letting it lie to you.
summary: How Facebook ran thousands of memcached servers serving billions of requests per second. The paper covers look-aside caching, leases that prevent stale sets and stampedes, regional pools, cold-cluster warm-up, and cross-region invalidation driven by the MySQL commit log. It is the practical manual for caching at scale.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Invalidate by deleting, never by setting, and drive deletions from the database's commit log.
Leases solve both stale sets and thundering herds.

title: The Tail at Scale (2013)
subtitle: Jeffrey Dean & Luiz André Barroso · CACM
lego: In a model with a thousand pieces, the slowest piece sets the pace.
summary: In a fan-out service, rare slow responses (the p99 tail) become the common case for users. The paper catalogues the causes (shared resources, garbage collection, queueing) and techniques to tolerate them: hedged requests, tied requests, micro-partitioning, selective replication, and putting slow machines on probation.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Don't try to eliminate variability. Build systems that are tail-tolerant.

title: Virtual CAD Tools for Architecture
subtitle: Excalidraw · Miro · Eraser · draw.io · the C4 model
lego: Digital LEGO Designer: lay out the whole model on screen before you buy a single brick.
summary: Sketch system topologies before spending money on cloud infrastructure. Excalidraw has a fast hand-drawn feel and is great for interviews. Miro is a collaborative whiteboard. Eraser turns text into diagrams (diagram-as-code) and has cloud icons. draw.io is free and precise. The C4 model gives you zoom levels (context, containers, components, code) so diagrams stay readable.

sections.title: Practice routine
items: For every Build card, draw it from memory in under 10 minutes, then compare it with the card.
Use one colour per brick family, matching this app: compute orange, storage blue, networking green, glue purple.
Label each arrow with the protocol and whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.

title: Map the Traffic Flow
subtitle: Four questions for every diagram
lego: Trace one peg's journey through the whole model with your finger.
summary: Take any system you use (a food-delivery app, your company's checkout, this flashcard app) and draw a single request's journey from the user's thumb to durable storage and back.
steps: Where does data enter? DNS, the CDN or edge, the load balancer or API gateway. Mark auth and rate limiting here.
Where is it computed? Which stateless services handle it, and which calls are synchronous?
Where does it halt? Queues and streams: what is buffered, for how long, and who drains it?
Where is it cached? Browser, CDN, the Redis tier, in-process. For each, what TTL and how it is invalidated.
Where is it permanently saved? The source-of-truth database or object store, how it is replicated, and how it is backed up.
Finally, circle every single point of failure in red and write the fix next to it.

sections.title: Self-check
items: Can you say the p99 latency budget of each hop?
What happens to an in-flight request if each box dies right now?

title: The 45-Minute Design Framework
subtitle: From a blank page to a defended design
lego: The instruction-booklet order: sort the pieces, build the base, add the details, then stress-test.
summary: You're handed a vague prompt like 'Design Instagram' and a whiteboard. Walk through a repeatable sequence that produces a scoped, estimated, defensible design in about 45 minutes.
steps: Requirements (5 minutes): the functional core (3–5 features) and the non-functional targets: scale, latency, availability, and the consistency each feature needs.
Estimates (5 minutes): users, read and write QPS, peak, and storage per year. Decide whether it is read-heavy or write-heavy.
API (5 minutes): the main endpoints or events, with request and response shapes and idempotency.
Data model (5 minutes): entities, access patterns, and the choice between SQL and NoSQL, with the partition key.
High-level design (10 minutes): snap the bricks together and trace the read path and the write path.
Deep dive (10 minutes): the hardest part, such as fan-out, hot keys, consistency or matching. Offer alternatives and choose one.
Wrap-up (5 minutes): bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring and alerting, and what you'd build next.

sections.title: Habits of strong candidates
items: State the trade-offs out loud: 'I'm choosing X over Y because…'
Start simple, then evolve: a single server, then the scaled version.

links.title: The System Design Primer: How to approach a system design interview question

title: Project 1: Build a URL Shortener
subtitle: API endpoint + hash generator + fast key-value store
lego: Your first real MOC: three bricks and one working model on your own table.
summary: Ship a working URL shortener on a free tier: POST a long URL and get a short code; GET the code and get redirected. Then measure it and make it faster.
steps: Compute: one HTTP service (a Cloudflare Worker, AWS Lambda behind a function URL or API Gateway, or a container on Fly.io or Cloud Run).
ID generator: base62-encode a counter (Redis INCR) or a random 7-character code with a conditional insert to reject collisions.
Key-value store: Upstash Redis, DynamoDB (on-demand), or Cloudflare KV storing code → URL.
Add caching: in-process LRU or edge cache headers for hot codes. Compare 301 and 302.
Add rate limiting per IP on POST and a click counter that is sent asynchronously (a queue or waitUntil).
Load-test it with k6 or hey. Record p50 and p99 before and after the cache in Notes (N).

sections.title: Stretch goals
items: Custom aliases with a uniqueness guarantee. Expiring links using TTL.
A click analytics dashboard fed from an event stream.

title: Project 2: Image Thumbnail Generator
subtitle: Object storage → event → serverless → object storage
lego: Drop a big picture brick in one bin and watch a tiny robot place a miniature copy in the next bin.
summary: Upload an image to an object storage bucket. A background event notification triggers a serverless function that resizes it and saves the thumbnail to another bucket or prefix, all without a server of your own.
steps: Create two buckets (or prefixes): uploads/ and thumbnails/. Writing output to a different place prevents an infinite trigger loop.
Give the client a presigned PUT URL from a tiny API so the image goes straight to storage.
Configure an S3 event notification (ObjectCreated), optionally through SQS for buffering and retries, to invoke a Lambda function.
The function downloads the image, resizes it (Sharp or Pillow) to several sizes, and writes them under thumbnails/{key}.
Record metadata (the original key, sizes, status) in a table, and show a gallery that reads the thumbnails through a CDN.
Upload the same file twice and upload a corrupt file. Confirm idempotency and that failures land in a DLQ.

sections.title: Stretch goals
items: Upload 1,000 images at once and watch concurrency, throttling and cost.
Switch the trigger to EventBridge and fan out to a second consumer, such as image labelling.

links.title: Tutorial: Using an Amazon S3 trigger to create thumbnail images

title: Project 3: Flash-Sale Order Queue
subtitle: A mini version of Example B that you can break
lego: Rebuild the toy-store ticket slot on your desk, then send a stampede at it.
summary: Build a tiny checkout: an API that accepts orders with an idempotency key, a queue, and a worker that writes to Postgres at a controlled rate. Then load-test it with a simulated flash sale.
steps: API (container or function): validate the order, do an atomic stock reservation in Redis, and enqueue {order, idempotencyKey}.
Queue: SQS, RabbitMQ in Docker, or a Postgres table used with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
Worker: an INSERT with UNIQUE(idempotency_key), a fake payment call with random failures and delays, and an acknowledgement only on success.
Blast it with 50× normal load using k6. Watch queue depth, worker throughput and database connections.
Kill the worker mid-run and restart it. Verify there are no lost or duplicated orders.

sections.title: What you should observe
items: API latency stays flat while the queue absorbs the spike.
The database's write rate stays at the worker's pace, not at the traffic's pace.

links.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

title: Chaos Engineering
subtitle: Break it on purpose, in daylight, with a hypothesis
lego: Deliberately pull a brick out of your model to see whether it wobbles, holds, or collapses, before a child's elbow does it for you.
summary: Chaos engineering means experimenting on a system to build confidence that it withstands turbulent conditions. Define the steady state (for example successful checkouts per minute), form a hypothesis ('if a cache node dies, checkouts stay within 5%'), inject a real-world fault, keep the blast radius small, and compare. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances so teams must design for it.

sections.title: Fault menu
items: Kill an instance, container or availability zone. Crash or fail over the database.
Add latency or packet loss, fill the disk, exhaust connections, skew the clock, revoke credentials.

sections.title: Tools
items: Toxiproxy (latency and timeouts between services), tc netem (network faults on Linux), Chaos Mesh (Kubernetes), AWS Fault Injection Service.

links.title: Chaos Engineering (Basiri et al., IEEE Software 2016)

title: Drill: The Database Crashes
subtitle: Does the app fail gracefully, or fall over completely?
lego: Yank out the bottom drawer while builders are still reaching into it.
summary: With your mini-project under steady load, stop the primary database (docker stop postgres, or trigger a managed failover). Observe what happens to incoming traffic, then patch the holes.
steps: Write the hypothesis: 'Reads keep working from cache or a replica, writes queue up, and there are no 500s at the edge.'
Start load (k6 at a steady rate) and a dashboard of error rate, p99 latency and queue depth.
Kill the database. Watch: do requests hang (no timeout), return 500s instantly, or degrade?
Restore it. Watch: does the app reconnect on its own, or does it need a restart because the connection pool is dead?
Patch and repeat until the result matches the hypothesis.

sections.title: What should happen
items: Short connect and query timeouts, so there are no thread pile-ups.
The circuit breaker opens: serve cached reads and show a friendly 'saving…' for queued writes.
The health check stays shallow, so the load balancer doesn't eject every app server because the database is down.

sections.title: Common holes
items: No timeout (a default of infinity), connection pools that never re-validate, and retry storms on recovery.

title: Drill: The Cache Layer Goes Down
subtitle: Does the backend drown in database calls?
lego: The arm's-reach shelf collapses, and suddenly every builder is digging in the heavy bottom drawer at once.
summary: With your app serving a read-heavy load at a 95%+ cache hit rate, stop Redis, or flush it, to simulate a cold restart. Measure how much load hits the database and whether it survives.
steps: Record the baseline: the cache hit ratio, database QPS and database CPU.
Flush or stop the cache under load, and watch database QPS jump by roughly 1 / (1 − hit rate). A 95% hit rate means about 20× the load.
Note whether the database saturates, latency explodes, or the app times out and retries, which makes it worse.
Patch it: request coalescing (single-flight), a short in-process L1 cache, load shedding on low-priority reads, and gradual cache warming.
Repeat, and confirm the database stays under about 70% CPU during a cold start.

sections.title: The lesson
items: A cache that the database can't survive without is really a hidden dependency. Size the database for the cold-cache case, or protect it.

title: Drill: Inject Artificial Latency
subtitle: A slow dependency is worse than a dead one
lego: One builder in the chain starts working in slow motion. Does the line wait politely, or does everyone pile up behind them?
summary: Add 500 ms to 2 s of latency (and some packet loss) between your service and one dependency, such as payments or the database, using Toxiproxy or tc netem. Observe thread and connection exhaustion and cascading slowness.
steps: Put Toxiproxy between the app and the dependency, and add a latency toxic of 1,000 ms ± 300 ms.
Watch in-flight requests, pool usage and p99 latency upstream. Do unrelated endpoints slow down too?
Add timeouts (from the dependency's p99), bulkheads (a separate pool), and a circuit breaker with a fallback.
Add retries with capped exponential backoff and jitter, and check that they don't amplify the load.
Repeat, and confirm unrelated endpoints stay fast and the affected feature degrades cleanly.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Dead dependencies fail fast. Slow ones hold resources until everything is stuck. Timeouts are the first line of defence.

links.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

title: Drill: Poison Message & Queue Backlog
subtitle: When the buffer tray overflows
lego: One malformed piece jams the machine, and the tray behind it keeps filling up.
summary: In your order-queue project, publish a message that always makes the worker throw an error, then double the producer rate beyond worker capacity for 10 minutes. See what happens to the queue, and to your users.
steps: Send the poison message. Does it retry forever and block a worker? Configure maxReceiveCount and a DLQ.
Alert on DLQ depth greater than zero, and build a redrive or replay path once the bug is fixed.
Overload the producers. Chart queue depth and the age of the oldest message against time.
Autoscale workers on backlog per worker, capped at the database's safe limit, and shed or delay low-priority messages.
Decide what the user sees when the ETA exceeds a threshold: an honest wait time, or reject at the edge.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Queues hide overload until they don't. Monitor the age of the oldest message, not just the count.

title: Drill: Lose an Availability Zone
subtitle: Static stability
lego: Knock an entire table over. Does the model on the other tables keep standing without any rebuilding?
summary: Simulate losing one of three availability zones: terminate its instances, and block its subnets or database replica. Can the remaining zones carry full traffic without any control-plane action, such as launching new instances?
steps: Pre-provision about 50% headroom per zone (with 3 zones, each runs at ≤ 66% so 2 zones can carry 100%).
Fail the zone: the load balancer health checks eject its targets, and the database fails over to a standby in another zone.
Measure the error spike duration, the failover time of the database and cache, and whether autoscaling was needed.
Verify there are no cross-zone hard dependencies, such as a single NAT gateway or a single-zone cache.
Write up the recovery time actually measured compared with your target, in Notes (N).

sections.title: The lesson
items: Design so that surviving a failure never requires the control plane to be healthy.
